Are there more statues of men named John than of women in London? Of 2364 identifiable memorials: 102 Johns (4%) vs 284 statues of women (12%). The claim is refuted for London. 557 memorials (24%) have no gender that clears the confidence threshold.

In England’s grand capital, dear,
More Johns than dames, it appears.
For each woman of might,
A John’s in plain sight,
Confirming our gendered-statue fears.

Caption: How are London’s memorials split by the gender of who they commemorate? One row per category, from memorials combined from Wikidata, OpenStreetMap and Historic England; records are merged only when they are close together and name the same subject. “Mixed” statues show a woman together with a man; the headline counts them as statues of women (276 Female + 8 Mixed = 284). “Unknown” means no gender reached the confidence threshold (see Reference). “Unnamed” records (1696) have no name or subject at all, so they are listed but left out of every percentage; percentages are of the 2364 identifiable memorials.

  • Finding
  • Overlap
  • Code

The campaign Statues for Equality claims that:

  • “The percentage of women’s statues in the UK that aren’t mythical or royal is approximately 3%”
  • “More statues of men named John dotted around the country than of women!”

Our London data: Found 102 statues named John/Jon/Jean (4%) vs 284 women statues (12%, including 8 of a woman with a man). 557 statues (24%) have unknown gender. Shares are of 2364 identifiable statues; 1696 records with no name or subject are not counted.

Validation: the claim that there are “more statues of men named John than of women” is refuted by this London dataset.

  • Men named John: 102 (4%)
  • Women: 284 (12%), of which 276 depict only women and 8 a woman together with a man

Percentages are of the 2364 identifiable memorials; 1696 records with no name or subject are not counted. The campaign’s claim is UK-wide; this dataset covers London only.

The two counts can overlap. A statue of a John together with a woman, such as “Katherine Mansfield and John Middleton Murry”, counts once as a John statue and once as a statue of a woman.

  • How Gender Is Decided
  • Data Sources
  • About
  • Session Info

Many records name the object, not the person: “Statue of Sir John Millais in North Forecourt of Tate Gallery”. We first read the subject from that text (here “Sir John Millais”).

If first names and titles cannot decide it, we ask Wikidata whether the subject is a person and, if so, their sex. An exact name match scores 1 and a partial match 0.7.

A gender is used only when its confidence is at least the classification threshold, currently 0.9. The same threshold applies to first-name predictions. It is set in one place, inst/extdata/params.csv; setting it to 1 keeps only certain answers, and the rest stay Unknown.

Caption: Did every data source respond, and how many rows did each return? ok means the fetch succeeded; an unavailable source is recorded with its reason rather than counted as empty. wikidata_people is the person lookup used to decide gender for subjects the name rules cannot (see How Gender Is Decided).

  • Wikidata: statues and public art in London, via SPARQL.
  • OpenStreetMap: memorials and statues, via the Overpass API.
  • Historic England / GLHER: heritage records.
  • Code: statuesnamedjohn on GitHub, pipeline in R/tar_plans/.

This dashboard compares memorials in London honouring three groups:

  1. Men named John: how common one male first name is among commemorated figures.
  2. Women of any name: gender representation in public memorials.
  3. Dogs, and animals generally: a quirky baseline.

Every number on these pages is computed by the targets pipeline; the Code tab on each card shows the pipeline step that produced it.
